blocks.text: Walk any street in Ibadan, Onitsha or Kaduna and you will see a grey tank on a pole. That distribution transformer is the last step of the national grid: it takes thousands of volts from the 11 kV line and delivers about 240 V to compounds and shops. Without it, every kettle and phone charger in the street would be destroyed — or the cables from the power station would have to be absurdly thick.

blocks.markdown:
A **transformer** changes the size of an alternating voltage using electromagnetic induction. It has no moving parts.

Two coils — the **primary** (input) and the **secondary** (output) — are wound on a soft-iron core. An alternating current in the primary produces a changing flux in the core. That changing flux links the secondary and induces an alternating e.m.f. there.

For an **ideal** transformer (no energy losses):

$$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{I_p}{I_s}$$

- If $N_s > N_p$, then $V_s > V_p$: a **step-up** transformer.
- If $N_s < N_p$, then $V_s < V_p$: a **step-down** transformer.

Power is conserved in the ideal case: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$. Raising the voltage therefore lowers the current in the same ratio.

blocks.title: A transformer needs a.c.
blocks.text: A steady d.c. primary current produces a steady flux, so ΔΦ/Δt = 0 and nothing is induced in the secondary. That is why the national grid is a.c., and why a phone charger first uses the a.c. mains before any rectification to d.c.

blocks.title: Finding the secondary voltage
blocks.prompt: A step-down transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 50 turns on the secondary. The primary is connected to a 240 V a.c. supply. Assuming the transformer is ideal, calculate the secondary voltage.

steps.text: Check: Ns is one-tenth of Np, so Vs must be one-tenth of 240 V. The transformer is stepping down, as expected for a device such as a laptop adapter.

rows: Thick copper wire of low resistance
Induced currents circulating in the core
Energy used in reversing the magnetisation of the core each cycle
Soft-iron core with a narrow hysteresis loop
Some primary flux does not link the secondary
Wind the coils close together, or one on top of the other, on a closed core
blocks.caption: Real transformers are typically over 95% efficient, but WAEC still expects you to name each loss and its remedy.

blocks.markdown:
### Why power is transmitted at high voltage

Electrical power $P = IV$. For a given power, **raising $V$ lowers $I$**. The heat wasted in the transmission cables is $I^2 R$, so a smaller current means far less waste.

That is the whole strategy of the grid:

1. Generate at a few kilovolts (a typical station output).
2. **Step up** at the station to 132 kV or 330 kV for the long TCN lines.
3. **Step down** in stages (33 kV, 11 kV) until the pole transformer outside a house delivers 240 V.

A numerical feel: 100 kW sent at 250 V needs 400 A; the same 100 kW at 25 kV needs only 4 A. The $I^2 R$ loss falls by a factor of $100^2 = 10\,000$ if the cable resistance is unchanged.

items: High voltage on the transmission line is not what you use at home — a chain of step-down transformers brings it down before the service cable enters the compound.
Current in the home wiring is then moderate, so cables can be thin enough to handle and cheap enough to install.
The same $P = IV$ argument is why a step-up transformer has fewer secondary turns carrying a smaller current of thicker wire on the primary, and vice versa for step-down.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Write Vs/Vp = Ns/Np first, then rearrange. Swapping primary and secondary is the most common arithmetic error. For losses, pair each name with its fix: laminations for eddy currents, soft iron for hysteresis, thick copper for I²R. And the reason for high-voltage transmission is always I²R in the cables — not 'so that the voltage can travel further' as a vague slogan.

points: For an ideal transformer, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is, and Vp Ip = Vs Is.
Step-up means Ns > Np; step-down means Ns < Np. Transformers work only on a.c.
Copper loss is cut with thick copper; eddy currents with a laminated core; hysteresis with soft iron; flux leakage by close windings on a closed core.
Power is transmitted at high voltage so that the current is small and I²R heating in the cables is small.
The grid steps up at the generating station and steps down, finally on the street-pole transformer, to about 240 V for homes.
